notes: History bank is overall very high quality — strong story-led stems, mostly Tier-1 named-thing answers, named figures in nearly every question, communist death tolls counted honestly. Flags concentrate on: (1) Drama-Available violations where dramatic stems yield label/date/place answers, (2) cross-tier duplicate clusters where same answer appears 2-5 times across tiers, (3) a few factual issues, (4) Tier-5 BANNED labels (battle names, place names, dates, country names) used as primary answers.

flags.stem_preview: On a hot July day in Philadelphia in 1776, delegates from 13 American colonies adopted a document written mainly by 33-year-old Thomas Jefferson, declaring themselves independent of Great Britain. What date is celebrated as Independence Day in the United States?
flags.answer_preview: July 4 1776
flags.issue: Pure date recall (Tier-5 BANNED in HISTORY_TEMPLATES §1). Anti_rote-adjacent. Answer is the date already implied in the stem.
flags.suggested_fix: Rewrite to ask the gap between independence-VOTE (July 2) and Declaration-SIGN (July 4) — the actual cool wonder fact — or ask for John Adams's now-famously-wrong prediction that July 2 would be the celebrated date.

flags.stem_preview: Early on a Sunday morning, Japanese carrier-based planes attacked the United States Pacific Fleet at its base in Hawaii without warning, killing 2,403 Americans and pulling the United States into World War II. President Roosevelt called the date 'a day which will live in infamy.'
flags.answer_preview: December 7 1941
flags.issue: Classic Drama-Available violation per HISTORY_TEMPLATES §1 Test 3. Stem has the 'day of infamy' quote IN it AND asks for the bare date. The quote IS the Tier-1 cool fact (taught canonically at IDX 548 T3 with the pencil-edit story 'world history' → 'infamy'). Date-recall is anti_rote-adjacent.
flags.suggested_fix: Rewrite to ask about Roosevelt's pencil edit on the speech draft (already taught at T3 IDX 548 — promote a T1 version), or about Jeannette Rankin's lone 'no' vote on the war declaration (IDX 925 T5).

flags.stem_preview: On the afternoon of July 3 1863, in the last desperate Confederate attack at Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, General Robert E. Lee ordered about 12,500 Confederate soldiers across an open mile of ground straight into Union cannon and rifle fire. About half were killed, wounded, or captured.
flags.answer_preview: Pickett's Charge
flags.issue: Generic battle-label answer (Tier-5 BANNED). Stem has 12,500 men + open mile + half killed/captured drama; answer is the named-charge label. Lee's 'It is all my fault — your men have done all that men could do' confession (IDX 512 T3) is the stronger cool fact.
flags.suggested_fix: Rewrite to ask about Lee's on-the-spot confession to Pickett OR about Chamberlain's bayonet charge at Little Round Top on the day before (IDX 563 T3). Currently a label answer.

flags.stem_preview: In October 1962 American spy planes photographed Soviet missile sites being built in Cuba — 90 miles from Florida. For 13 tense days President John F. Kennedy and Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev faced each other across the brink of nuclear war. The Soviets eventually backed down.
flags.answer_preview: The Cuban Missile Crisis
flags.issue: Drama-Available violation (Tier-5 BANNED event-label answer). Stem has 'brink of nuclear war' + named figures + 13 days drama; asks for the event name. Better: the secret Turkish missile trade (IDX 540 T3) or Kennedy calling it a 'quarantine' instead of 'blockade' (IDX 860 T5).
flags.suggested_fix: Rewrite to ask what Kennedy called the naval cordon (quarantine, to avoid casus belli), or what Khrushchev secretly got in exchange (Turkish Jupiter missile removal).

flags.stem_preview: In June 1967 Israel, surrounded by Arab armies threatening invasion, launched a surprise attack that destroyed the Egyptian, Syrian, and Jordanian air forces on the ground in the first three hours. The entire war ended in six days...
flags.answer_preview: The Six-Day War
flags.issue: Generic war-name label answer (Tier-5 BANNED). The '6 days' is in both stem AND answer (gives it away — skim-tell). Drama-Available violation.
flags.suggested_fix: Rewrite to ask about Operation Focus / Moked (the codename for the lightning air strikes), or what Israel captured in the six days (Sinai, Golan, West Bank, East Jerusalem).

flags.stem_preview: On September 15 1950, three months into the Korean War, U.N. forces under American General Douglas MacArthur launched a daring amphibious landing far behind North Korean lines at a difficult port with 30-foot tides...
flags.answer_preview: Inchon, South Korea
flags.issue: Place-name answer (Tier-5 BANNED). Drama-Available violation: 30-foot tides + behind enemy lines + 'reversed the war' drama in stem, asks for venue.
flags.suggested_fix: Rewrite to ask about the 4-hour daily tide window that made the landing nearly impossible, the codename Operation Chromite, or what percentage of MacArthur's staff opposed the plan before the gamble paid off.

flags.stem_preview: From 1958 to 1962 Chinese Communist leader Mao Zedong launched a campaign to industrialize China overnight using mass peasant labor — backyard furnaces, mass irrigation projects, and forced grain collection. It produced the deadliest famine in human history.
flags.answer_preview: The Great Leap Forward
flags.issue: Generic campaign-name label answer (Tier-5 BANNED). The 30-45M death toll IS the cool fact and IS taught at IDX 588 T3 / IDX 953 T5 — but stuffing 'deadliest famine in human history' into the stem and asking for the label name is the textbook §1 anti-pattern.
flags.suggested_fix: Rewrite to ask about the four-pests campaign (sparrows killed → locust plagues), backyard furnaces destroying farm tools, or the death-toll number (30-45M).

flags.stem_preview: In April-July 1994 the ethnic-majority Hutu government of the central African nation of Rwanda organized the massacre of about 800,000 ethnic-minority Tutsis (and moderate Hutus) over about 100 days. The killers used mostly machetes, encouraged by radio broadcasts naming individuals to murder.
flags.answer_preview: The Rwandan Genocide
flags.issue: Generic event-label answer (Tier-5 BANNED). Stem has machetes + radio broadcasts naming individuals (a horrifying Tier-1 detail) + 800,000 in 100 days. The cultural term 'Inyenzi' ('cockroaches' — what Hutu Power called Tutsis) is the Tier-1 cool fact, taught at IDX 760 T4.
flags.suggested_fix: Rewrite to ask what the radio broadcasts called the Tutsi target ('Inyenzi' / cockroaches), or to ask about RTLM (Radio-Télévision Libre des Mille Collines) and its role.

flags.stem_preview: Summer 1666: plague closed Cambridge and the 23-year-old Isaac Newton went home to his mother's farm at Woolsthorpe. In a single 'year of wonders' he invented calculus, the laws of motion, and the law of universal gravitation. According to legend, Newton was sitting in the garden when one specific event made him think...
flags.answer_preview: An apple fell from a tree
flags.issue: Cross-tier duplicate cluster — Newton-1666-apple appears at IDX 234 (T1), IDX 462 (T2), IDX 492 (T3), IDX 899 (T5). The apple is asked 4 times. Plus IDX 0 (T1) uses near-identical stem opener to ask 'annus mirabilis'. Per HISTORY_TEMPLATES §1.5 'cross-tier same-answer duplicates is a real failure mode of parallel-tier-agent rebuilds.'
flags.suggested_fix: Keep ONE apple question (the lowest-tier T1). Rewrite IDX 462/492/899 to use other Newton facts — alchemy obsession (IDX 816), Halley funding Principia from the failed-fish-book (IDX 663/834/885), Newton-Leibniz dispute (IDX 476/633/665), 'on the shoulders of giants' Hooke jab.

flags.stem_preview: From February 23 to March 6, 1836, about 200 Texan defenders held a fortified Spanish mission in San Antonio against the much larger Mexican army of Antonio López de Santa Anna. All the defenders died including frontier figures Jim Bowie and Davy Crockett.
flags.answer_preview: The Alamo
flags.issue: Generic-label answer (place name, Tier-5 BANNED) when 200 defenders died + Crockett + Bowie drama in stem. Travis's line-in-the-sand (IDX 869 T2) is the Tier-1 vivid action; 'Remember the Alamo!' (IDX 69) is the Tier-1 named rally cry.
flags.suggested_fix: Either remove this question (already covered by IDX 69 + IDX 525 + IDX 525) or rewrite to ask about Bowie's deathbed defense (knife under bed) or about who carried the news of the fall.

flags.stem_preview: On January 1, 1863, President Abraham Lincoln issued an executive order during the Civil War declaring enslaved people in Confederate-controlled territory legally free. The order changed the war's character — from a war for the Union to a war for the Union AND emancipation.
flags.answer_preview: The Emancipation Proclamation
flags.issue: Document-name label answer. Stem contains all the substance; answer is just the title. Stronger options: the political timing after Antietam (IDX 858 T5), the strategic limitation (didn't free border-state slaves), or specific phrases.
flags.suggested_fix: Rewrite to ask about the Proclamation's striking scope-limitation: it freed slaves ONLY in Confederate-held territory (not border states, not Union-held South) — exposing it as a war measure. This is the wonder reveal.

flags.stem_preview: On December 17, 1903, on the windswept dunes of Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, two brothers from Dayton, Ohio made the first sustained, controlled, powered flight of a heavier-than-air craft. The first flight lasted about 12 seconds and covered 120 feet. Who made the flight?
flags.answer_preview: Orville and Wilbur Wright
flags.issue: Name-the-creator (anti_rote-adjacent). Wright Brothers' names are common knowledge. Wright-1903 Cluster: IDX 21 (T1) and IDX 320 (T2) and IDX 440 (T2) and IDX 495 (T3) and IDX 674 (T4) and IDX 900 (T5) all use the same 12-sec/120-ft fact. 6-tier duplicate cluster.
flags.suggested_fix: Consolidate the Wright Brothers cluster. Keep T1 + T4/T5 (which use unique angles like 3-axis control). Rewrite the middle tiers to test different facts: Orville-vs-Wilbur coin toss (IDX 81 has bicycle shop), Lord Kelvin's 'impossible' statement, four flights that morning (Wilbur's fourth covered 852 feet).

flags.stem_preview: On May 17, 1954, the U.S. Supreme Court unanimously ruled that racially segregated public schools were unconstitutional, overturning the 1896 Plessy v. Ferguson 'separate but equal' doctrine. Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote the opinion.
flags.answer_preview: Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka
flags.issue: Case-name label answer. Stem has 'unanimously' (the cool fact!) + Warren + overturned Plessy drama. The 9-0 unanimity Warren built behind the scenes is the more memorable fact.
flags.suggested_fix: Rewrite to ask about the 9-0 unanimity Warren strategically achieved (he kept the decision delayed until he could get every Southern justice on board) OR the named plaintiff (third-grader Linda Brown, walked past her neighborhood white school to a black school).

flags.stem_preview: On the clear morning of September 11, 2001, 19 hijackers from al-Qaeda took control of four passenger airliners. Two struck the twin towers of the World Trade Center in New York; one struck the Pentagon; one crashed in a Pennsylvania field after passengers tried to retake the plane. About 3,000 people died. Who led al-Qaeda at the time?
flags.answer_preview: Osama bin Laden
flags.issue: Drama-Available violation. Twin towers + Pentagon + 3,000 dead + passenger uprising in stem; asks for bin Laden's name (common knowledge). Stem also wastes the Flight 93 passenger uprising — 'Let's roll' (Beamer, IDX 154 T1) is the Tier-1 cool fact.
flags.suggested_fix: Rewrite to ask about Flight 93 passenger Beamer's Lord's Prayer + 'Let's roll' moment (IDX 343 T3) OR what the iconic helicopter-rope-ladder photo actually showed (the Pittman Apartments — a CIA officers' residence, misidentified as the embassy for decades, IDX 710 T4).

flags.stem_preview: On January 30-31, 1968 — during the Tet (lunar new year) ceasefire — communist North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces launched simultaneous attacks on over 100 cities and military bases throughout South Vietnam, including the U.S. embassy in Saigon. American forces beat back the attacks but the offensive shattered U.S. confidence.
flags.answer_preview: The Tet Offensive
flags.issue: Generic offensive-name label answer (Tier-5 BANNED). 100 cities + US embassy attacked + shattered US confidence drama in stem; asks for the campaign name.
flags.suggested_fix: Rewrite to ask about Walter Cronkite's Feb 27 1968 'mired in stalemate' broadcast (LBJ reportedly said 'If I've lost Cronkite, I've lost middle America'), or the strategic paradox (tactical US victory, strategic NV win).

flags.stem_preview: In September 480 BC, with Athens evacuated and the Persian fleet of about 1,200 ships hunting the smaller Greek fleet (~370 ships), Athenian commander Themistocles tricked the Persians into entering a narrow strait where their numbers would not help them. The Greeks destroyed about 200-300 Persian ships and lost about 40...
flags.answer_preview: The Salamis Strait — between Salamis island and Attica
flags.issue: Place-name answer (Tier-5 BANNED). Drama-Available violation: 'trick' + named figures in stem; asks for the strait name. Sicinnus's slave-message ploy (IDX 552 T3, IDX 948 T5) is the Tier-2 vivid action — the actual trick.
flags.suggested_fix: Rewrite to ask about the slave Sicinnus's false message to Xerxes (the actual trick — taught at T3/T5 but missing at T2). Currently a venue-name answer.

flags.stem_preview: On April 26, 1986, Reactor No. 4 at a Soviet nuclear power plant in Ukraine exploded during a safety test, releasing the largest atmospheric release of radioactive material in human history. The Soviet government's first instinct was to deny anything had happened. The world only learned about the disaster three days later...
flags.answer_preview: Chernobyl
flags.issue: Place-name answer (Tier-5 BANNED). Stem has explosion + denial + 3-day delay drama; asks for the plant name. The 'first detected in Sweden' story (IDX 142 T2 / IDX 759 T4) is the Tier-1 named-place reveal.
flags.suggested_fix: Rewrite to ask where in the West radiation was first detected (Forsmark in Sweden — taught at IDX 142/759) OR what 'Liquidators' (IDX 239) refers to. Currently a plant-name answer.

flags.stem_preview: Joan of Arc was the illiterate peasant girl from Domrémy who at 17 convinced the French dauphin Charles to give her command of an army. She broke the English siege of Orleans in May 1429 and saw Charles crowned king at Reims that July. Captured by the Burgundians in 1430, she was sold to the English and tried by a French...
flags.answer_preview: May 30 1431, age 19 — burned at the stake in Rouen's market square
flags.issue: Drama-Available violation per USER MEMORY's canonical example. Joan stem with burned-alive + 19 + ashes drama but answer is venue+date+age. HISTORY_TEMPLATES §1 Test 3 explicitly cites Joan-Rouen as a fail. The canonical fix is 'Threw her ashes into the Seine' (IDX 254 T2). Joan-cluster: 7 questions at IDX 7, 221, 235, 254, 487, 667, 893.
flags.suggested_fix: Rewrite IDX 487 to ask about the ashes-into-Seine (currently only at T2), or Joan's last word at the stake ('Jesus' per chronicler accounts), or her trial's specific 'cross-dressing' charge. The current question repeats the burned-at-Rouen failure mode.

flags.stem_preview: Thomas Edison invented the phonograph in 1877 — a tin-foil cylinder rotated under a stylus that vibrated with the speaker's voice. Edison made the first recording himself, reciting four words from a children's nursery rhyme into the horn. What four words did Edison record?
flags.answer_preview: 'Mary had a little lamb'
flags.issue: FACTUAL ERROR: 'Mary had a little lamb' is FIVE words, not four. Stem says 'four words.' Internal contradiction within the question.
flags.suggested_fix: Fix stem: 'a line from a children's nursery rhyme' or 'a few words from'. The 4-word claim is wrong on the face of it.

flags.stem_preview: Francis Drake, English privateer, set sail from Plymouth in December 1577 in his 100-ton ship the Pelican, which he renamed mid-voyage to honor his patron Sir Christopher Hatton. He raided Spanish ports along the Pacific coast of South America, captured immense treasure, and returned to England in September 1580 — the...
flags.answer_preview: Circumnavigate the globe — first was Magellan's expedition, completed by Elcano in 1522
flags.issue: Stem appears truncated; the implied question is 'first English to circumnavigate' or 'first to fail to be first at X' — but the answer is phrased confusingly. Verify stem coherence — the question may be asking what Drake was NOT first to do.
flags.suggested_fix: Verify the full stem (it cuts off in preview). If asking 'what was Drake NOT the first to do?' the answer is fine. The phrasing should be clearer about whether circumnavigation was the achievement Drake DID accomplish (yes, second-ever), or whether he wasn't first at it (correct).

flags.stem_preview: On August 8 1974 President Richard Nixon announced his resignation in a televised address from the Oval Office, effective at noon the next day. He became the first U.S. president to resign. The scandal that brought him down had begun with a June 17 1972 break-in at a specific Washington building. What was that building called?
flags.answer_preview: The Watergate complex — Democratic National Committee headquarters
flags.issue: Cross-tier duplicate of IDX 342 T2 — same Watergate-naming question at different tiers. The building name IS a Tier-1 named thing (suffix '-gate' for every later scandal is the wonder hook), but two questions for the same fact is over-representation.
flags.suggested_fix: Consolidate: keep T2 (IDX 342), rewrite T3 IDX 544 with the famous '18.5-minute gap' on the tapes, 'I am not a crook' speech, Mark Felt = Deep Throat reveal (2005), or Saturday Night Massacre.

flags.stem_preview: Pope Julius II forced the Sistine Chapel ceiling commission on Michelangelo in 1508 over his protests — he insisted he was a sculptor, not a painter. Working alone on a custom scaffold he designed himself, he painted 5,000 square feet of fresco over four years. The job left him with a specific physical change he wrote about in a sonnet to his friend...
flags.answer_preview: His neck stayed permanently bent upward — he could only read letters held above his head
flags.issue: Cross-tier 5-deep duplicate cluster: IDX 5 (T1), IDX 258 (T2), IDX 658 (T4), IDX 830 (T5), IDX 883 (T5) all use the Pope-forced-Sistine-Michelangelo opener. IDX 658, 830, 883 all give the same 'neck bent permanently' answer.
flags.suggested_fix: Consolidate Sistine cluster. Keep T1 (head-bent-back posture in IDX 5) and one higher tier with the neck-curse. Rewrite the others using OTHER Sistine facts: Creation of Adam's finger-gap, Michelangelo painting his face onto Saint Bartholomew's flayed skin, the patches Daniele da Volterra later painted over the nudes ('Il Braghettone' — the breeches-maker).

flags.stem_preview: Bach's St. Matthew Passion premiered in Leipzig in 1727 and was then virtually forgotten for over a century. The 20-year-old Felix Mendelssohn conducted its public revival in Berlin on March 11 1829, sparking the modern Bach renaissance. Mendelssohn knew the score because, six years earlier, a family member had given him a manuscript copy as a 14th-birthday present...
flags.answer_preview: His grandmother Bella Salomon — for his 14th birthday
flags.issue: Cross-tier near-duplicate of IDX 481 (T3) and partial overlap with IDX 270 (T2), IDX 826 (T5), IDX 878 (T5). Bach-revival cluster is 5-deep with overlapping facts.
flags.suggested_fix: Consolidate the Bach-revival cluster. Keep T2 (basic story) and T5 (the 400-singer reorchestration). Rewrite T3/T4 with other Bach-revival facts: Mendelssohn's Jewish heritage giving Christian Passion a deliberately syncretic note, the cut of 1/3 of the score to fit the Romantic-concert format, Zelter's mentorship.

flags.stem_preview: Brunelleschi began work on Florence's cathedral dome in 1420 — solving a problem that had defeated builders for over a century. He worked without scaffolding from below; the opening was too vast to span. The dome rose course by course as he laid roughly 4 million bricks in a specific interlocking pattern that locked each course...
flags.answer_preview: Herringbone — vertical bricks set between horizontal courses to lock each ring as the dome rose
flags.issue: Cross-tier 4-deep duplicate: Brunelleschi-herringbone appears at IDX 4 (T1), IDX 256 (T2), IDX 500 (T3), IDX 661 (T4). HISTORY_TEMPLATES §1.5 Brunelleschi worked-example shows ONE event should yield FIVE DIFFERENT cool-fact answers, not the same answer 4 times.
flags.suggested_fix: Consolidate to ONE tier (T1 or T2). Rewrite IDX 500/661 with the OTHER Brunelleschi facts the templates document EXPLICITLY: the egg demonstration (IDX 479 T3 has this), the lost-Roman-formula 130-year delay, the goldsmith original trade, the still-standing-largest-masonry record (IDX 892 T5).

flags.stem_preview: The Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe — whose meticulous naked-eye observations made Kepler's laws possible — sported a famous facial replacement for most of his adult life. He had lost the original part in a duel with a fellow Danish nobleman in December 1566, fought over a disagreement about which of them was the better...
flags.answer_preview: A prosthetic nose, likely brass with silver inlay
flags.issue: Cross-tier duplicate: Tycho-nose appears at IDX 3 (T1), IDX 222 (T1), IDX 477 (T3), IDX 666 (T4), IDX 842 (T5). 5 questions about the same nose, with IDX 3 and 477 and 666 essentially identical setup-and-payoff.
flags.suggested_fix: Consolidate the Tycho-nose cluster. Keep T1 + T5 (which uses the 'gold/silver/copper alloy' specifier). Rewrite T3/T4 with other Tycho facts: his elk dying from beer, his observatory Uraniborg on Hven (IDX 220), supernova 1572 (IDX 824), Tycho's pet jester Jeppe sleeping under the table, exploded bladder death after holding it at the imperial banquet.

flags.stem_preview: On November 9 1989 — less than 30 months after Reagan's June 12 1987 Brandenburg Gate speech demanding 'tear down this wall' — the Berlin Wall opened. Within weeks Germans on both sides were taking it down with hammers and chisels. Communist regimes across Eastern Europe collapsed in rapid succession through the rest of...
flags.answer_preview: Nicolae Ceaușescu of Romania — shot December 25 1989
flags.issue: FACTUAL ERROR in distractors: ALL three distractors claim other communist leaders were 'shot' in December 1989. FALSE — Honecker was NOT shot (deposed Oct 1989, died Chile 1994); Husák resigned Dec 1989 (died 1991, natural causes); Zhivkov resigned Nov 1989 (died 1998). The distractors fabricate executions that never happened.
flags.suggested_fix: Replace distractors with truthful alternatives: 'Honecker of East Germany — deposed Oct 1989, died Chile 1994' / 'Husák of Czechoslovakia — resigned Dec 1989, died 1991' / 'Zhivkov of Bulgaria — resigned Nov 1989, died 1998'. Currently the distractors are factually false — a 'no fabrication' violation per HISTORY_FRAMEWORK §7.

flags.stem_preview: In 1324 Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire in West Africa, made the pilgrimage to Mecca. His caravan brought so much gold — distributed as alms and tribute — that the price of gold in Egypt collapsed and took roughly a decade to recover. Modern estimates of Mansa Musa's net worth (adjusted for inflation) suggest he m...
flags.answer_preview: About 10 to 12 years
flags.issue: Mansa Musa cluster: IDX 156 (T1), IDX 414 (T2), IDX 615 (T3), IDX 783 (T4), IDX 1003 (T5). 5 questions about the same caravan-crashes-gold-economy. IDX 156 and 783 and 1003 all ask the recovery-decade.
flags.suggested_fix: Consolidate. Keep one tier asking the decade. Rewrite others with the gold-caravan specifics (60,000 men, 12,000 slaves carrying gold, 80-100 camels with 300lbs each — IDX 615 has this), or the architect Es-Saheli he brought back from Mecca to build the Djinguereber Mosque.

flags.stem_preview: In 1274 and again in 1281 Kublai Khan — Mongol emperor of China — launched massive sea invasions of Japan with combined Chinese-Korean-Mongol fleets and armies. Both invasions were destroyed by major typhoons that struck while the invasion forces were at sea or anchored offshore. The Japanese named the typhoons with a Japanese word still used today...
flags.answer_preview: Kamikaze — 'divine wind'
flags.issue: Cross-tier duplicate with IDX 409 (T2). Same Kublai-invasion-of-Japan + kamikaze-typhoon setup yields same answer. T4 should use deeper material.
flags.suggested_fix: Rewrite T4 to use the WWII reuse of 'kamikaze' (suicide pilots, IDX 575) tied back to its origin — OR the specific scale (140,000 men in 1281 — largest naval invasion until D-Day) — OR the 2001 underwater archaeology that found mass shipwrecks proving the story.

flags.stem_preview: In the late 12th and early 13th centuries, under the Zagwe dynasty King Lalibela of Ethiopia, eleven monolithic churches were carved out of solid volcanic rock in the highlands of north-central Ethiopia. The churches are unique because they were not built up from a foundation but excavated downward — the builders start...
flags.answer_preview: Carved DOWNWARD into the bedrock from above — the churches sit below ground level
flags.issue: Cross-tier duplicate: Lalibela carved-downward appears at IDX 171 (T1), IDX 794 (T4), IDX 1006 (T5). Three near-identical questions.
flags.suggested_fix: Consolidate. Keep T1 (introductory) + T5 (with named king + volcanic-tuff specifier). Rewrite T4 with the post-Saladin pilgrimage motive (IDX 423 has this at T2), or the cross-cut courtyards forming Greek-cross plans, or the specific church names (Bete Medhane Alem is the largest).

flags.stem_preview: Bach's St. Matthew Passion premiered at Leipzig's Thomaskirche in 1727. By the time Bach died in 1750 the Baroque style had been eclipsed by the Classical, and his enormous output was largely forgotten outside small German Lutheran circles. His son Wilhelm Friedemann's widow famously sold manuscripts as scrap paper.
flags.answer_preview: Felix Mendelssohn
flags.issue: T5 question with too-easy answer (just identify Mendelssohn). The Bach-revival cluster IDX 270/481/660/826/878 has 5 questions. This T5 is the weakest — name-recall when richer details exist (the 400-singer reorchestration in IDX 878 is the genuine T5).
flags.suggested_fix: Consolidate. Keep IDX 878 as the T5 (substantive 400-singer/score-cut detail). Cut IDX 826 OR rewrite to ask about Mendelssohn's specific cut decisions or the Sing-Akademie chorus.

flags.stem_preview: By late January 1943 the German 6th Army was trapped at Stalingrad on the Volga, encircled since November by Operation Uranus, starving and frostbitten. Field Marshal Friedrich Paulus surrendered to the Red Army on January 31, becoming the first German field marshal ever taken prisoner alive. About 91,000 starving Germans were captured...
flags.answer_preview: About 5,000 — only one in eighteen of the captured 6th Army survived Soviet captivity
flags.issue: Cross-tier duplicate of IDX 653 (T3). Both ask the 91,000 captured → ~5,000 survived statistic. Same answer at two tiers.
flags.suggested_fix: Keep T3 (lower tier). Rewrite T5 to focus on Paulus's later anti-Nazi broadcasts (IDX 358 T5 has this) or the 57,000 prisoner march through Moscow (IDX 935 T5).

flags.stem_preview: Lincoln's Gettysburg Address opens with the four-word phrase 'Four score and seven years ago.' A 'score' is twenty years, so 'four score and seven' equals 87. Lincoln spoke on November 19 1863. Subtracting 87 takes him not to the year a U.S. citizen of 1863 might have expected — 1776 — but to the year that, for Lincoln...
flags.answer_preview: The Declaration of Independence in 1776 — not the Constitution of 1787
flags.issue: Strong T5 question — uses arithmetic puzzle as wonder hook, with substantive Lincoln-style natural-rights interpretation. Solid.
flags.suggested_fix: Keep — but verify the math (Nov 19 1863 - 87 = 1776). Lincoln chose 1776 (the natural-rights founding) over 1787 (the Constitution that compromised with slavery). The substance is correct.

flags.stem_preview: On March 21 1861, three weeks before Fort Sumter, Confederate Vice President Alexander Stephens addressed a large crowd at the Athenaeum in Savannah, Georgia. His speech laid out what he said was the founding principle of the new Confederate government — the principle he said distinguished it from the federal Constitution...
flags.answer_preview: Slavery — the new government rested on 'the great truth that the negro is not equal to the white man'
flags.issue: Cross-tier duplicate of IDX 313 (T2) and IDX 689 (T4). Cornerstone Speech taught three times.
flags.suggested_fix: Consolidate. Keep T2 + T5 (since they teach the Confederate-states-own-declaration substance the framework calls for). Rewrite T4 IDX 689 with related Confederate-states-secession-declarations (Mississippi's secession declaration is even more explicit) or the Confederate Constitution's explicit slavery protection clause.

flags.stem_preview: In September 490 BC the Athenian army of about 10,000 hoplites, with about 1,000 Plataeans, met a Persian invasion force of perhaps 20,000-25,000 on the plain of Marathon north of Athens. The Athenian general Miltiades thinned his center and reinforced his wings; he charged at the run across the last 200 yards to close...
flags.answer_preview: A runner named Pheidippides reportedly ran the roughly 25 miles from Marathon to Athens to announce the victory and then dropped dead
flags.issue: Marathon-Pheidippides cluster (8 questions): IDX 31 (T1) names him; IDX 241 (T2) gives the quote; IDX 564 (T3) ran-26-miles; IDX 740 (T4) quote variant; IDX 839 (T5) Nike-version; IDX 947 (T5) repeat of the run-and-died. Very saturated.
flags.suggested_fix: Consolidate the Marathon-Pheidippides cluster. Keep one per tier with DIFFERENT angles: T1=name (IDX 31), T2=quote (IDX 241), T3=phalanx-running-charge (IDX 102 already covers phalanx but here add the run-charge under arrow fire), T4=Herodotus's actual report (Pheidippides went to Sparta, not Athens — the run-to-Athens story is conflation), T5=the 1896 Olympic marathon's creation.
